paras: The death of Herbert Brooks occurred on July 31, 1920, when Brooks, a Black Bahamian held on a charge of assaulting an elderly white woman in Miami, Florida, died near Ormond while officers were taking him by train to Jacksonville. Officials said he leaped from the train, but Bahamian residents of Miami said he had been lynched, and their protest led the mayor to call out the National Guard. An autopsy demanded by the British vice-consul was reported to find nothing to support that charge, and Black papers added their own comment to the wire story.

According to Associated Press dispatches, a white woman, fifty-five by one account, was attacked in her Miami home on Friday, July 30, 1920. Herbert Brooks was arrested as a suspect, and the woman was later reported to have identified him as her assailant. Brooks was a British subject from the Bahamas, one of several hundred Bahamian residents whom the wire called "alien negroes." The Baltimore Afro-American described Miami as a city where no Black person could own an automobile.

On the night of July 30 a crowd began to form in Miami, and the Evening Star reported that 1,200 "infuriated white men" surrounded the jail and demanded the prisoner. Fearing mob violence, the sheriff had Brooks sent out of Miami that night for Jacksonville, for identification or for safe keeping by different accounts.

Shortly after noon on July 31, Brooks died at or near Ormond. A telegram from Sheriff Monroe of St. Lucie County said Brooks had jumped from the moving train and killed himself; later dispatches said he jumped to escape the officers.

When the body arrived in Miami on August 2, more than 400 Bahamian residents demonstrated and threatened vengeance, saying Brooks had been killed by a mob rather than by a leap from the train. Mayor William Pruden Smith, with the adjutant general's sanction, called out forty guardsmen to patrol the Black section with the police.

At the demand of British Vice-Consul A. A. H. Hubbard, the county physician, Dr. E. K. Jaudon, performed an autopsy, which according to the Associated Press "revealed nothing of a sensational nature." The Washington Times said the examiners found nothing to justify the Bahamians' version; the Afro-American wrote that the autopsy "confirmed an accidental death." On August 3 the troops were demobilized after Brooks's body was put aboard a steamer for burial in Nassau, and Florida dispatches reported no disorder. No report of grand jury action on the death or of arrests among the jail crowd was found.

White newspapers ran the story as Associated Press copy, in Florida and in papers from Washington and Richmond to Chattanooga. Early headlines such as "Negro Killed by Jump From Train" and "Train Leap Is Fatal" gave the officers' account as fact, and later copy said the Bahamians only "professed to believe" in a lynching. Coverage of the aftermath centered on the threat of Black disorder, under headlines such as "Race Troubles in Miami Feared" and "Call Florida Troops to Guard Miami From Mob."

The Chicago Whip and the Omaha Monitor reprinted the wire account under headlines stressing the threat to Miami from "400 Bahamans" and "Negroes." The Monitor, however, added a line of its own: "It is noticeable how quickly troops can be summoned when 'Negro disorder' threatens; but white mobs are given ample time to act."

The Baltimore Afro-American, headlining "Lynching Charged," said nearly one-fourth of the Black population armed and threatened to wipe out white Miami, and that crowds met the body. In an item dated August 13, the Tulsa Star said the Bahamians charged the police with "an unwarranted killing" of Brooks and called him innocent.

Brooks's death was disputed: the account of a leap came from the officers who held him, the autopsy both presses cited was by the county physician, and the Bahamians blamed a mob or, per the Tulsa Star, the police. Reports also differ on where Brooks was arrested and on his burial, placed in Nassau by Florida dispatches but described by the Afro-American as a crowded funeral. The Tulsa Star dated the demonstration to "last Sunday" in an August 13 item; the contemporary AP reports put it on August 2.

reader.title: Death of Herbert Brooks
bases: A white crowd surrounded the Miami jail demanding Brooks (A2), who died in officers' custody the next day; officials said he leaped from a train (A3), while Bahamian residents said he was lynched (A7, A11, A17).

Brooks died and a crowd of 1,200 white men had demanded him at the jail (A2), but every report of the death itself gives the officers' account that he jumped from a train (A3, A16), and the claim that a mob killed him appears only as the belief of Bahamian residents, without details (A7, A17).

Many reports agree that Brooks died on the way to Jacksonville (A1, A2, A3), but the officers' account of a leap from the train is contradicted by the Bahamian residents' charge of a lynching (A7, A11, A17) or a police killing (A19).

accounts.label: Sheriff's telegram / AP wire
accounts.gist: Brooks, being taken to Jacksonville for safe keeping because the sheriff feared mob violence, jumped from the moving train at Ormond and killed himself.

accounts.label: Bahamian residents of Miami
accounts.gist: Brooks did not leap from the train but was killed by a mob; he had been lynched.

accounts.label: Tulsa Star item
accounts.gist: The Bahamians charged the local police with an unwarranted killing of Brooks and declared him innocent of the charge.

accounts.label: Autopsy by county physician
accounts.gist: The autopsy revealed nothing of a sensational nature, found nothing to justify the Bahamians' version, or 'confirmed an accidental death'.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Negro Killed by Jump From Train' and 'Train Leap Is Fatal' gave the officers' account as fact and called the lynching charge what the Bahamians 'professed to believe'.
Aftermath headlines centered on the threat of Black disorder: 'Race Troubles in Miami Feared', 'Call Florida Troops to Guard Miami From Mob'.
The Chicago Whip ran the AP copy unchanged under 'Miami Threatened by 400 Bahamans'.
The Omaha Monitor added that troops are summoned quickly for 'Negro disorder' while 'white mobs are given ample time to act'.

The Baltimore Afro-American headlined 'Lynching Charged', gave the Black residents' charge and their armed mobilization, and described Miami's discrimination, while reporting the autopsy as confirming an accidental death.

versions.value: Jumped from the moving train and killed himself (sheriff's telegram, AP)
Killed by a mob / lynched (Bahamian residents)
Unwarranted killing by local police (Bahamians, per Tulsa Star)

conflicts.note: The jump account comes from officers holding Brooks; the autopsy cited against the lynching charge was by the county physician. No independent account of the death was found.

versions.value: Arrested as suspect in Miami, spirited away Friday night

conflicts.note: The earliest Miami-datelined reports, which describe the jail crowd, place him in Miami custody Friday night; 'arrested at Ormond' looks like a garbled later wire variant.

versions.value: August 2 (Monday), on arrival of the body
'last Sunday' in an item dated August 13

conflicts.note: The AP dispatches written at the time date it to August 2; the Tulsa Star item appears to be late.

versions.value: Body put aboard a steamer for Nassau for burial
Crowds met the body, attended the funeral and buried it with great ceremony

conflicts.note: The Afro-American does not say where the burial took place.
Other copies name Jaudon as the county physician; the Pensacola copy appears to conflate the two.

record_check.dossier: No paper names a county for Miami or Ormond; the only county named is St. Lucie, whose sheriff telegraphed the news of the death.
Attempted (crowd of 1,200 demanded Brooks at the jail) is reported; a completed lynching is only the Bahamian residents' charge, denied by officers and the autopsy reports.
Brooks was in officers' custody when he died; no report says a mob took him, only that Bahamians believed a mob killed him.
A crowd of 1,200 white men at the Miami jail; the alleged killers are unnamed, a mob per the Bahamians or the local police per the Tulsa Star.
Death on July 31; demonstration August 2. The August 8 value follows the Tulsa Star's late 'last Sunday'.

record_check.record: Brooks 'found dead' after being taken to Jacksonville; Guard called to the Negro settlement
record_check.dossier: He died en route near Ormond, by officers' account leaping from the train; he was not 'found dead'. Guard call-out and Bahamian protest are correct.

info: Brooks died July 31, 1920, shortly after noon; demonstration and Guard call-out August 2
Alleged assault, jail crowd and demonstration in Miami, Fla.; death at or near Ormond, Fla. ('Orond', 'Omond' in OCR)
Herbert Brooks, Black ('negro'), a British subject and native of the Bahamas ('West Indian' per the Afro-American)
Accused of assaulting (criminal assault upon) an aged white woman, aged 55 per one report, in her home in Miami
A crowd of white men surrounded the Miami jail Friday night and demanded the prisoner; Bahamian residents said a mob killed Brooks; the Tulsa Star says they charged the local police
Body put aboard a steamer for burial in Nassau; no disorder reported
